faqs.question: How long should a 2 line birthday wish be?
faqs.answer: About 96 characters, or 15 to 20 words. That is the median personal message length across 197 birthday pages on SubhSandesh, and 106 of those 197 came in under 100 characters. Anything shorter than about 60 characters usually loses the personal half.

faqs.question: Is a two-line birthday message too short to be polite?
faqs.answer: No. Short is the normal case, not a shortcut — 106 of 197 measured messages were under 100 characters. Politeness comes from the specific detail in line two, not from length. A vague 300-word message reads as less personal than a precise 96-character one.

faqs.question: What should the second line of a birthday wish say?
faqs.answer: One specific thing only: a memory, a trait with evidence, a promise, a running joke, or a plan with a day attached. Research on congratulation strategies finds the common pattern is the plain greeting overlapped with exactly one further strategy. Two things in line two makes it three lines.

faqs.question: Should a 2 line birthday wish include the person's name?
faqs.answer: Yes, in almost every case. The name costs you six or seven characters and it is the cheapest possible proof that the message was not copied. Skip it only when the message is going into a one-to-one chat where the name would sound formal.

faqs.question: Can I send the same two-line wish to more than one person?
faqs.answer: Not if it contains a real detail, which is the point of the second line. If a wish can go to two people unchanged, line two is generic and you should replace it. Line one can be identical for everyone; line two cannot.

faqs.question: Do emojis count towards the two lines?
faqs.answer: Visually yes, and each emoji takes roughly the width of a character on a phone. One at the end is fine. Three or more push the message onto a third line on most screens and start doing the work that your words should be doing.

faqs.question: Is a long birthday message better than a short one?
faqs.answer: Only for milestones and for repairing something. For an ordinary birthday, length does not correlate with care — the longest message recorded on a SubhSandesh birthday page ran 1,437 characters, and it is an outlier, not a benchmark. Most people write about 96 characters.

faqs.question: Does a two-line wish still work if I have missed the day?
faqs.answer: It works, but the second line has to acknowledge the delay rather than ignore it. A late wish that pretends to be on time reads worse than a late wish that says so plainly and then gets to the specific detail.

faqs.question: Can I put a two-line wish on a birthday page instead of sending it in chat?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the two lines stay two lines — the page carries the photo, the music and the private link around them. Bear in mind birthday pages average 11.2 views each, so it reaches one or two people closely rather than a crowd.

faqs.question: Are quizzes and games worth adding to a short birthday message?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Of 195 SubhSandesh birthday pages that added a quiz, only 28 had it played — 14.4%. The extras are fun to build and rarely opened, so the sentence is where the effort pays.

article.contentMarkdown:
# 2 Line Birthday Wishes That Fit How People Actually Write

A 2 line birthday wish runs about 96 characters — roughly 15 to 20 words. That is not a style preference, it is a measurement: across 197 personal messages written on SubhSandesh birthday pages, the median came in at exactly 96 characters, and 106 of those 197 messages sat under 100 characters. Two lines is already what people write when nobody is standing over them with a word count. The pages ranking for this phrase hand you 100, 125 or 185 options and not one of them says how long a birthday wish should actually be, which is the single thing you came to find out. This page gives you the length first, then five two-line shapes with the real character count printed beside each, a table of what fits at every length, and the case where two lines is the wrong call. Birthday pages are the fifth most-created page type on SubhSandesh: 198 of 3,024 pages.

## What is a 2 line birthday wish?

A 2 line birthday wish is a message short enough to read in a single glance — an opening greeting plus one specific thing about the person. In practice that is two sentences, or one sentence and a short second clause, landing somewhere between 60 and 120 characters.

The second line is the whole difference. "Happy birthday" on its own is a greeting. "Happy birthday. This is the year I actually come to Pune instead of promising to come to Pune." — 94 characters — is a message, because only one person on earth could have received it.

The organising idea here is length, not relationship. A two-line wish for a cousin and one for a colleague are built the same way and differ only in the detail dropped into line two. On SubhSandesh birthday pages, 100% carry a written birthday wish and 99.5% add a personal message on top, so the personal line is close to universal already.

## Why 96 characters is the number to aim at

The 96-character median comes from 197 personal messages on birthday pages created since April 2026. The longest single message in that set ran 1,437 characters. The distribution is lopsided towards short, which is what you would expect from people writing on a phone at eleven at night.

Real messaging corpora agree. In the [88milSMS corpus of over 88,000 authentic French text messages](https://journals.openedition.org/corpus/4852) collected over 13 weeks in 2011 and described by Panckhurst, Lopez and Roche in the journal *Corpus* in 2020, very short messages of under 15 characters made up 16.5% of everything sent — and the average message-reduction rate was under 10%, meaning people were not abbreviating much. They were simply writing short and writing it properly.

Short also does measurable work on the writing itself. Gligorić, Anderson and West studied Twitter's 2017 switch from 140 to 280 characters and [found that a length constraint makes people write more tersely](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/15079), using more abbreviations and contracted forms and fewer definite articles — and their initial evidence was that tweets written to fit the old 140-character limit were *more* successful than same-length tweets written once the limit was lifted. Two lines is that constraint, applied to a birthday.

## Five two-line shapes, with the character count for each

Every one of these is a greeting plus exactly one specific thing. The counts are the real character counts of the examples as printed, spaces included.

### 1. Greeting plus one specific memory

Name the moment, not the friendship. "Happy birthday, Aarav. Hostel mess was survivable only because you were in the queue next to me." — 96 characters. Best for friends and siblings who share a defined period with you: college, a job, a house. It fails on someone you met recently: you will reach for a memory, find a generic one, and a generic memory reads worse than none.

### 2. Greeting plus one thing you admire

State a trait and the evidence for it in the same breath. "Happy birthday, Ma. You still pick up on the first ring, and I have never once had to wait for you." — 99 characters. Best for parents, teachers, bosses and anyone senior to you, where a shared joke would be awkward. It fails when the trait is vague: "you're always so kind" could go to forty people unchanged.

### 3. Greeting plus a promise for the year ahead

Point forward instead of back. "Happy birthday. This is the year I actually come to Pune instead of promising to come to Pune." — 94 characters. Best for long-distance friends and relatives you keep meaning to visit, and it is the only shape that works when your shared history is thin. It fails if you have sent the same promise last year, in which case it reads as a habit rather than a plan.

### 4. Greeting plus a running joke

Use the joke you already have, never a new one. "Happy birthday, Sneha. Twenty-nine again, and the maths gets harder to defend every single year." — 96 characters. Best for close friends and cousins where the teasing is established and mutual. It fails in a group chat and it fails on anyone sensitive about age, so this is the shape most likely to land wrong with an audience you have misjudged.

### 5. Greeting plus a plan with a date in it

Turn the wish into an appointment. "Happy birthday. Coffee at your place on Sunday, and I am bringing the cake this time. No arguments." — 99 characters. Best for people in the same city that you genuinely intend to see, and it is the highest-converting shape because it requires a reply. It fails the moment you do not mean it, because an unkept plan is a worse memory than a plain greeting.

## What goes in line one and what goes in line two

There is research on the internal structure of a congratulation, and it maps neatly onto two lines. Saleem, Saleem and Aziz ran a discourse completion test with 120 participants — 30 British English speakers and 90 Pakistani ESL learners across three social classes — and [found the most frequent congratulation strategy was the illocutionary force indicating device](https://sfleducation.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40862-022-00134-9), the plain explicit "congratulations", followed by *overlapped* strategies combining two, then an offer of a good wish and an expression of happiness.

Read that as an instruction. Line one is the explicit device: "Happy birthday." Line two is the second strategy you overlap onto it — the good wish, the happiness, the memory, the plan. Two lines is not a truncated long message; it is the second-most-common natural shape a congratulation takes, written out.

Brief messages in a fixed space are older than texting. Julia Gillen's study of [ten British Edwardian picture postcards from a collection of three thousand](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/65539/), published in the *Journal of Sociolinguistics* in 2013, describes a cheap channel with several deliveries a day carrying brief multimodal messages, and draws the connection to claims made about digital practice today. People have been fitting a relationship into a few lines for well over a century.

## Two lines against every other length

Here is what each length band actually holds, with the SubhSandesh figure that goes with it.

| Wish length | Characters | Words, roughly | What the SubhSandesh data shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| One line | Under 50 | 6–8 | All 198 birthday pages carry a written birthday wish |
| Two lines | 96 at the median | 15–20 | 106 of 197 personal messages are under 100 characters |
| Short paragraph | 100–300 | 20–50 | The other 91 of 197 messages run 100 characters or longer |
| Long letter | Over 300 | 50+ | The longest single message recorded is 1,437 characters |

The takeaway is that two lines is the majority case and the long letter is the outlier, not the ideal — 106 of 197 people landed under 100 characters without being told to.

If you want the wish to sit somewhere better than a chat thread, a [birthday page for a friend](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-friend) gives the two lines a cover photo, a song and a private link, and the two lines stay two lines. For someone closer, the [best friend birthday page](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-bestfriend) does the same job with a different tone.

## When two lines is the wrong choice

Two lines is wrong for a milestone. A 60th birthday, a first birthday after a hard year, or a parent's birthday you missed last time all carry a weight that 96 characters cannot hold, and the recipient will read the brevity as effort withheld. Write the paragraph.

Two lines is also wrong when the relationship needs repair. A wish is not an apology and compressing both into one message does neither job.

And a caution about dressing the two lines up. On SubhSandesh, 195 of 198 birthday pages added a quiz — but only 28 had it played, 14.4%. Senders build games; recipients read the message and close the tab. Four pages were never opened at all. Extras do not rescue a vague line two.

One more inconvenient number: birthday pages average 11.2 views each against 12.2 site-wide, and only 2 of 198 ever passed 50 views. It is read closely by one or two people, which argues for writing well rather than writing more. Birthday pages are also made fast — median 0.9 hours from first save to last edit, 50.5% finished inside the hour — so two lines suits how people work. Pick a shape, drop in the one specific detail, and stop; [browse the full template library](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) if you want the format around it.

## Sources

- Panckhurst, R., Lopez, C. and Roche, M. (2020). "A French text-message corpus: 88milSMS. Synthesis and usage." *Corpus* 20. [journals.openedition.org/corpus/4852](https://journals.openedition.org/corpus/4852)
- Gligorić, K., Anderson, A. and West, R. (15 June 2018). "How Constraints Affect Content: The Case of Twitter's Switch from 140 to 280 Characters." *Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media* 12(1). [ojs.aaai.org](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/15079)
- Saleem, A., Saleem, T. and Aziz, A. (12 April 2022). "A pragmatic study of congratulation strategies of Pakistani ESL learners and British English speakers." *Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education* 7(8). [sfleducation.springeropen.com](https://sfleducation.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40862-022-00134-9)
- Gillen, J. (2013). "Writing Edwardian postcards." *Journal of Sociolinguistics* 17(4), 488–521. [eprints.lancs.ac.uk](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/65539/)

SubhSandesh figures come from a read-only probe of the birthday page collection run on 26 August 2026 (n=198 pages, n=197 personal messages).

failed.item: Any paywalled citation records that only the abstract was read
failed.why: Recorded here rather than in the body. Two of the four sources were verified from abstract-level metadata only: the Springer Open landing page for Saleem, Saleem & Aziz (2022) returned a bot challenge, so its title, journal, date, CC BY licence and full abstract were verified through the Crossref API record for 10.1186/s40862-022-00134-9; and the open post-print PDF of Gillen (2013) at eprints.lancs.ac.uk was not text-extractable through the fetch pipeline, so only the repository landing page abstract was read. Both are open access, so a reader can check them; closes when a text-extractable copy of each full text can be read end to end.

failed.item: No source URL appears in more than 2 posts in this batch; no domain in more than 3. **One exception: the date/festival reference** (e.g. a panchang for the festival date and muhurat). Every post in a festival batch may verify the same date — that is a fact-check, not a citation, and it has no cap. It only earns a place in `citation` where the post actually states the time; a post that merely mentions the date keeps it out of `sources` and `citation` entirely.
failed.why: Passes as measured, but at the limit and worth re-checking before merge. journals.openedition.org stood at 2 uses across the corpus when measured on 2026-08-27 (2026-08-19-diwali/first-diwali-away-from-family and 2026-08-26-birthday/birthday-wishes-for-nephew, both different URLs), so this post takes it to exactly 3 — the cap, not over it. Other agents are still writing; if another post adds an openedition URL, this one breaches and the 88milSMS citation would have to be replaced. Closes on a final corpus-wide re-measure at merge time.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine asked "how long should a birthday wish be" has, on this SERP, nothing to cite: every ranking page publishes between 100 and 185 options and none of them states a length. This post answers with a measured number — 96 characters median across 197 real messages, 106 of 197 under 100 — that no competitor can publish, and pairs it with the congratulation-strategy and message-corpus research that explains why that number is the natural shape rather than a compromise. The honest limits: n=197 is small, the data starts April 2026, there is no per-relationship or per-language breakdown, and subhsandesh.in has far less domain authority than the established writing and lifestyle publishers on this SERP, so ranking is a question of months and backlinks rather than of this page being right. The likelier near-term win is citation by an answer engine that needs a number, not a top-three blue link.
